Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

The library gives us two folding tables, and we bring the boards, clocks, pencils, and a clipboard. I usually arrive at six fifteen, even though the first games start at seven, because the room needs a little time to settle. The chairs go along the long wall, and the boards sit far enough apart that a player can stand up without bumping the next game. The board table is about six feet from the door, so people coming in can find us without walking through a game.

First, I check the ladder sheet against the notebook from the last meeting. The sheet shows each player name, current rung, last opponent, and the date of the last result. I keep a second page for people who have asked to join but have not played yet, because it is easy to promise someone a place and then lose their phone number. The ladder has twenty-four regular names right now, and we cap it at thirty so the room stays manageable. If somebody has missed several weeks, I leave their name in place and ask privately whether they still want to take challenges. We do not drop people just because they had a busy month.

Next, I set out four boards and clocks and test every clock before anyone arrives. Two of the clocks are old analog ones, and the black hand sometimes catches near twelve, so I move it around once and listen for the click. I set the standard game at thirty-five minutes per player with a five-second delay and write that on the small card by the entrance. New players sometimes assume we use a faster setting because they have seen blitz games online. The card helps avoid that awkward conversation later. If a clock will not start, I swap it out rather than ask players to keep tapping the button.

At the door, I greet people and ask them to sign beside their name the first time they come. I also ask whether they are comfortable using a clock and whether they want help finding an opponent. I do not ask for a rating because our ladder is based on results here and not on an outside number. A newcomer once told me, “I only know the rules from playing my uncle,” and I said, “That is enough to start. We can explain the local challenge rule before the game.” If somebody is nervous, I show them where the restroom and water fountain are so they do not have to leave the room wondering which hallway to use.

When most people have arrived, I read the challenge order from the sheet. The player may challenge someone one to three rungs above them, and a player who is challenged gets first choice of color for that game. If both people agree, they can play a friendly game instead, but it does not change the ladder result. I explain those points slowly because people often remember the range as one to two rungs. The challenge has to be accepted that evening or arranged for another date. Both players should tell me before leaving so I can mark it as pending. We do not treat a missed message as a forfeit.

1. Opening the room and matching players. I start with the highest unfinished challenge and then work down the page. When two people are ready, I point out their names and ask each of them to confirm the color and time control before the clocks begin. The white player presses the clock only after making a move, and the black player does the same after replying. I remind them that a legal move should be completed before the clock is pressed. If a piece is knocked over, they can stop the clock and reset the position together. A disagreement about the position means they call me over instead of trying to settle it while both clocks run.

During play, I stay available but try not to hover. I do not comment on a move or suggest a plan, even if I can see a hanging queen; that is part of playing your own game. I can answer a procedural question, such as whether a player may write down moves, but I do not advise on the position once a game has started. If someone needs a break, they may pause the clock only for a clear practical reason and tell me what happened. Last week, a chair leg broke during a game, so we stopped both clocks, moved the board to another table, and restarted the same position after checking the move record. The players were fine with that and finished without rushing.

After a game ends, I ask both players to report the result together, and then I enter the date and score in the notebook. A win lets the challenger move above the person they beat, and the other names shift down one place. A draw leaves both players where they are unless they agree to schedule a rematch outside the ladder. I have had people remember the same game differently, so I ask them to check the final position and agree on the score before I change the sheet. If there is still a disagreement, I write down both accounts and leave the ladder unchanged until we can speak calmly the next week. No one should feel pressured to produce a result just to keep the evening moving.

Before we close, I check that every board has a recorded result or a note saying the game is unfinished, and that both players know what happens next. I write the next meeting date as the following Thursday because the library is closed this week, and I tell everyone to check the notice on the front door before coming back. I collect pencils and clocks first, then stack the boards with the pieces in their bags. The library staff need the tables returned to the original layout, so we put the chairs back along the wall and take our paper with us. I keep the ladder sheet in my folder rather than leaving names in the room.
